title: Needs and wants
job: Say what you want and don't want
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Wanting to DO something is voglio plus a bare infinitive: Voglio mangiare. There is no word for "to" in it, and nothing may stand in the gap — neither a nor di.
Negation is ONE word in ONE place: non, straight in front of the verb, and nothing else in the sentence moves — Non voglio il caffè. English needs a "do not" helper that Italian has no equivalent of.

The indefinite article picks its shape from the sound that follows it: un before most masculine nouns (un caffè, un libro), uno before a masculine noun starting with s + consonant or with z (uno zaino, uno studente), una before a feminine noun (una pizza), un' before a feminine noun starting with a vowel (un'amica).
The plural is a change of the last vowel and never an added -s: libro → libri, pizza → pizze, studente → studenti. -o becomes -i, -a becomes -e, and -e becomes -i whatever the noun's gender.
An adjective normally FOLLOWS its noun and agrees with it: una casa grande, un libro italiano, una pizza italiana. English puts the adjective in front and never inflects it, so both halves are new.
vorrei is the polite want — "I would like" — and in this course it is one of the two things that carry politeness. voglio is direct without being rude: a friend at a table, a child to a parent.
volere names its person in the ending, like every verb so far: voglio (I) · vuoi (you) · vuole (he, she).

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Want a coffee" — the "I" is inside voglio

words.note: volere — to want. The ending names the person: voglio (I) · vuoi (you) · vuole (he, she). It is direct without being rude; the softer vorrei arrives in S08.
The masculine indefinite article, and the everyday one: un caffè, un libro, un amico. It changes to uno before a masculine noun starting with s + consonant or with z.

sentences.trap: English chooses between "a coffee" and "some coffee" by how much you mean. Italian's indefinite article does not care about the amount — it changes for the SOUND of the noun behind it.
sentences.sound: VO-lyo. The gli is one sound, the ly of "million" pressed together — the g is never heard on its own.

variations.changed: voglio → vuoi and a question mark: the same want, asked
swap what you want — un holds, because libro is masculine too
non in front of the verb, and nothing else moves

mistake.why: uno stands only before s + consonant or z. Before caffè the article is un.

sentences.usage: Asking for something plainly — at a table with friends, or at home.
sentences.mnemonic: un is the short one, for the words that need no help.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Want a pizza" — una because pizza is feminine

words.note: The feminine indefinite article: una pizza, una casa. Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel it loses its own vowel and joins on — un'amica.
Feminine: la pizza (one) · le pizze (more than one). The plural is the last vowel changing from -a to -e.

sentences.trap: English "a" never changes shape. Italian's does, and gender is what decides: una for a feminine noun, un for most masculine ones.
sentences.sound: PIT-tsa. The double z is a doubled "ts", held twice as long as a single one — Italian's doubled consonants are heard, not just written.

variations.changed: more than one: the noun's -a becomes -e, and the article goes plural with it
voglio → vuoi: the same want, asked of you
the adjective goes behind the noun and agrees with it — italiana

mistake.why: pizza is feminine, so the article is una: Voglio una pizza.

sentences.usage: Ordering, or saying what you feel like eating.
sentences.mnemonic: una ends in -a because pizza does.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Want a backpack" — uno, because zaino starts with z

words.note: The masculine article for the awkward openings: a noun starting with s + consonant or with z takes uno, not un — uno zaino, uno studente. It is the same shift that gives the plural gli instead of i.
Masculine: lo zaino (one) · gli zaini (more than one). Its z is what pulls uno and lo in front of it.

sentences.trap: un is right nearly all the time, which is exactly why this one is missed. It is the noun's opening SOUND, not its meaning, that pulls uno.
sentences.sound: DZAI-no. Italian z at the start of a word is often a "dz", and -ai- is one glide, not two syllables.

variations.changed: voglio → vuoi: the same want, asked — and uno is untouched by it
an ordinary masculine opening, so un comes back
non in front of the verb; the article is untouched by it

mistake.why: A z at the start of the noun pulls uno: Voglio uno zaino.

sentences.usage: Shopping, or saying what you need for a trip.
sentences.mnemonic: uno is the long article for the words that start with a mouthful.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Not want the coffee" — one word does the whole negative

words.note: The whole negative, in one word, standing immediately in front of the verb: Non voglio, Non sono, Non mi piace. Nothing else in the sentence changes, and nothing else is added — Italian has no helper answering to English "do not".

sentences.trap: English builds a negative out of two pieces — do plus not — and neither has an Italian twin. Put non in front of the verb and stop.
sentences.sound: NON, one short syllable with an open o, and it leans onto the verb behind it: non voglio comes out in one breath.

variations.changed: swap what you are refusing — non does not move
another verb, same position: non goes in front of whatever the verb is
voglio → vuoi and a question mark — a negative question needs nothing added either

mistake.why: non goes in FRONT of the verb, never after it: Non voglio il caffè.

sentences.usage: Turning something down without explaining yourself.
sentences.mnemonic: non stands guard in front of the verb.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Want eat" — there is no word for "to"

words.note: The plain form of the verb — what a dictionary lists. Italian's -are ending IS the English "to", so mangiare is already "to eat" and needs nothing in front of it.

sentences.trap: English "want to eat" has a "to" in it, and the hand reaches for a or di to fill the gap. After volere there is no gap: Voglio mangiare.
sentences.sound: man-JA-re. The gi is the j of "jam", one sound, and the final -e is pronounced.

variations.changed: voglio → vuoi: the infinitive behind it does not move at all
non in front of the verb — the infinitive stays where it is

variations.cue: I want to eat a pizza
variations.changed: the infinitive takes its own object, and the frame still holds

mistake.why: Nothing stands between volere and its infinitive — no di, no a. Voglio mangiare.

sentences.usage: Saying what you feel like doing, at any hour.
sentences.mnemonic: -are is the "to": mangiare is already "to eat".

sentences.cue: I want to drink a coffee

words.note: to drink. Its plain form ends in -ere rather than -are — the second of Italian's three verb classes — and after volere it stands bare, exactly as mangiare does.

sentences.trap: English can say "have a coffee" and mean drinking it. Italian will not: avere is for owning, and drinking is bere.
sentences.sound: BE-re, two clear syllables, and the single r is one tap of the tongue.

variations.cue: I don't want to drink the coffee
variations.changed: non in front, the two verbs untouched behind it

variations.cue: Do you want to drink a coffee?
variations.changed: voglio → vuoi: the want moves to you, the infinitive stays

variations.cue: I want to drink a beer
variations.changed: swap the drink — and una, because birra is feminine

mistake.why: No a. volere takes the bare infinitive: Voglio bere un caffè.

sentences.usage: Suggesting a stop at a bar, or saying what you are after.
sentences.mnemonic: bere is short because a drink is quick.

sentences.cue: I don't want to study today
sentences.glossEn: lit. "Not want study today" — nothing is added for the negative or the "to"

words.note: to study — an -are verb like mangiare, and it carries its own object: studiare l'italiano.

sentences.trap: Two English pieces are missing at once here, and both are missing on purpose: no "do" in front of the negative, and no "to" before the second verb.
sentences.sound: stu-DYA-re. The -dia- is one syllable, DYA, not dee-ah.

variations.changed: drop non and the sentence turns positive — nothing else moves
drop the time word: it was never holding the sentence together

variations.cue: Do you want to study Italian?
variations.changed: voglio → vuoi, and the infinitive takes an object of its own

mistake.why: No a between volere and its infinitive — and non is already doing all the negating this sentence needs.

sentences.usage: Saying no to a plan, with the reason left out.
sentences.mnemonic: Two English words vanish here: "do" and "to".

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Would-want a pizza" — the polite want

words.note: The polite want — "I would like". It is volere in another shape, and it is what you say across a counter or to someone you have just met. voglio is not rude; vorrei is simply softer, and in this course it is one of the two things carrying politeness.

sentences.trap: English softens a request from outside the verb — please, could I, would you mind. Italian can soften it inside the verb, and then the sentence needs nothing else.
sentences.sound: vor-REY. The double r is trilled longer than a single one, and -ei is one glide.

variations.changed: swap what you are asking for — un, because caffè is masculine
the direct want instead — fine among friends, blunt at a counter

variations.cue: I'd like to eat a pizza
variations.changed: vorrei takes a bare infinitive too, exactly as voglio does

mistake.why: vorrebbe is the polite Lei form, which this course does not teach. Speaking as yourself it is vorrei.

sentences.usage: Ordering, asking, or saying what you would like when you are not among friends.
sentences.mnemonic: The extra r in vorrei is the extra politeness.

sentences.cue: I want a bit of bread

words.note: "A bit of", and it is the everyday way to ask for some of something. The apostrophe is not decoration: po' is poco with its ending cut off, and the apostrophe is the cut. It never comes off, and it is always the straight one.
Masculine — il pane — even though it ends in -e, which is an ending both genders use. Like English "bread", it is not usually counted.

sentences.trap: English has two ways in — "some bread" and "a bit of bread" — and neither translates piece by piece. un po' di is one thing, learned whole.
sentences.sound: The apostrophe is a cut, not a sound: po' is simply "po", short. The three words run together — oon-po-DEE.

variations.cue: I'd like a bit of bread
variations.changed: voglio → vorrei: the polite want in front of the same phrase

variations.cue: I want a bit of music
variations.changed: swap what you want some of — un po' di never changes

variations.display: Non voglio un po' di pane
variations.cue: I don't want a bit of bread
variations.changed: non in front of the verb; the phrase behind it is untouched

mistake.why: po' keeps its apostrophe — it is poco with the ending cut away, and the apostrophe is what says so.

sentences.usage: Asking for some of something at a table, without naming an amount.
sentences.mnemonic: po' is poco with its tail cut off, and the apostrophe is the scar.

words.note: Feminine: la casa (one) · le case (more than one). It covers both "house" and "home".
big. An adjective ending in -e has ONE shape for both genders — una casa grande, un libro grande — and goes to -i in the plural for both: case grandi, libri grandi.

sentences.trap: English puts the adjective in front of the noun and never changes it. Italian normally puts it behind and makes it agree — though grande, ending in -e, agrees only in number.
sentences.sound: CA-za and GRAN-de. The single s between two vowels is a z through much of the north and a plain s in Tuscany; both are standard.

variations.changed: an -o/-a adjective instead, so it agrees in gender too — italiana
a masculine noun, and grande does not move: -e adjectives have one shape
plural on both sides — case and grandi, and sono for "they are"

mistake.why: grande ends in -e and has one shape for both genders: una casa grande, un libro grande. There is no granda.

sentences.usage: Saying what you are after when the thing alone is not enough.
sentences.mnemonic: An -e adjective is lazy: it changes for number and not for gender.
